Your turn: Land use updates in the region

Sept. 4, 2026
By Stephanie Swensrude and Karen Unland

This week's roundup of calls for public engagement includes a public hearing about proposed changes to St. Albert's land use bylaw that would make it easier to build small-scale infill in mature neighbourhoods, as well as transit-oriented development along St. Albert Trail.

St. Albert council is set to hear from residents at a public hearing on Sept. 15 on changes to its land use bylaw that would address two out of seven initiatives it is expected to fulfill under the Housing Accelerator Fund from the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation. St. Albert intends to have 20% of new homes built along St. Albert Trail and within established neighbourhoods.

The first change would make it easier to build small-scale infill in established neighbourhoods. Administration proposes decreasing the minimum width for lots, enabling slightly narrower single-detached and semi-detached homes in neighbourhoods where they're already allowed. Administration was adamant that it is not making changes that would enable the type of infill in mature neighbourhoods that is regularly met with opposition in Edmonton. "What we're NOT doing is introducing six- or eight-plexes, nor changing regulations for parking, building heights, setbacks, and more," the city said.

Staff recommends amending the trail corridor commercial district to allow apartment buildings as-of-right, instead of requiring permission from a development planner. The district's maximum height would also increase by three metres to 25 metres, or about eight storeys.

The changes would also introduce a mixed-use, transit-oriented development district that could only be used along St. Albert Trail with a maximum height of about 15 storeys. The city intends to make it easier to build housing and mixed-use spaces within 800 metres of planned transit nodes on St. Albert Trail.

The proposed changes to the land use bylaw are among the initiatives St. Albert has committed to in return for $11.8 million in federal funding. It is also in the process of finalizing its housing affordability strategic plan based on its housing needs assessment report. Future initiatives include exploring how city-owned land can be used for housing and launching an online permit portal for developers. St. Albert is "making good progress" on its housing action plan, according to the CMHC's progress tracker.

Meanwhile, Fort Saskatchewan postponed voting on its renewed land use bylaw in August so it could have a more in-depth discussion on Sept. 3. That discussion led to a series of motions asking administration to bring back amendments related to various matters including density and height, which passed.

The proposed bylaw reduces the number of districts from 55 to 18, and regulates sites based on "built form" instead of uses — in other words, the shape and appearance of a building instead of what kind of activities are allowed there. However, each built form will still conform to a permitted list of activities. Administration said a land use bylaw based on what a building looks like is almost entirely unique in Alberta. "This approach ensures scale- and place-appropriate development and compatibility between the allowed activities, and streamlines the permitting process," Shree Shinde, the city's manager of current and long range planning, said in August. There will be a public hearing before council makes its final vote.

Leduc has extended the timeline on its land use bylaw renewal to allow for more public feedback. Residents told city staff that they want more housing options that are carefully integrated into establishing neighbourhoods, they want to keep current parking regulations in place, and they support having convenient and walkable places to gather and connect within neighbourhoods. A new draft is set to be presented in early 2027. And Morinville has begun engagement on its land use bylaw, with plans to consult the public in spring 2027.

Headlines: Sept. 4, 2026

Sept. 4, 2026
By Mariam Ibrahim
  • Construction has begun on an expanded habitat for Lucy the Elephant at the Edmonton Valley Zoo. The project, expected to be completed in 2027, will nearly triple her enclosure to about 70,000 square feet and add a new indoor facility and larger outdoor yard. The upgrades are intended to improve Lucy's comfort and care as she ages. The zoo is also exploring accreditation from theAssociation of Zoos and Aquariums, which would require meeting enhanced standards for elephant care and safety.
  • Edmonton city council's executive committee approved $114.58 million in climate-related actions for consideration during the city's four-year budget deliberations, while four no-cost measures can begin immediately. The plans include making city operations more energy-efficient, improving electrical-grid resilience with EPCOR and incorporating extreme weather into planning. Funding proposals for December include decarbonizing the city's vehicle fleet, supporting climate-resilient buildings and expanding facilities that provide relief during extreme heat, cold or smoke.
  • As more than 70,000 students return to school, the City of Edmonton is increasing police patrols at public transit hubs during weekday rush hours through Sept. 18. Peace officers and transit staff will also be stationed near post-secondary campuses and will attend student orientations to provide safety information and resources.
  • NorQuest College criminologist Dan Jones told Postmedia the decision by the Edmonton Police Commission to move meetings online and suspend public speaking could damage police legitimacy. The commission cited months of abusive and threatening behaviour for the temporary changes. Jones said he saw no extreme behaviour at a contentious July meeting and argued uncomfortable criticism is part of public oversight. Mayor Andrew Knack said public participation is an important part of the democratic process.
  • St. Albert Mayor Scott Olivieri criticized Edmonton Coun. Michael Janz for suggesting municipalities outside Edmonton are not doing enough to address homelessness and emergency shelter needs. Janz made the comments during an Aug. 25 public hearing on a proposal to convert a Hope Mission facility into a year-round emergency shelter, pointing to a lack of permanent shelter beds outside Edmonton. Olivieri called Janz's remarks "short-sighted" and said the issue is more complex than his comments suggest. Janz defended his position, saying shelter and addiction services should be distributed across the region.
  • Elections Alberta said it began mailing referendum special ballot packages after receiving about 225,000 requests, nearly four times the 2023 total. It said special ballot applications now close Sept. 25, and completed packages must arrive by 5pm on Oct. 16.

A moment in history: Sept. 4, 1947

Sept. 4, 2026
By Scott Lilwall

On this day in 1947, Edmonton's Great Western Garment Company was advertising for new workers.

GWG was once a massive name in the clothing industry. But when the company was founded in 1911, it started with just 15 workers and eight sewing machines. Alberta's first premier, Alexander Rutherford, along with Alfred E. Jackson and salesman Charles A. Graham, started it. The garment maker targeted farmers, ranchers, and other workers with affordable, durable clothing under the motto "They wear longer because they're made stronger."

Shortly after the company's founding, its staff unionized, forming Local 120 of the United Garment Workers of America at Edmonton. GWG recognized the union. Workers secured conditions like an eight-hour workday and a 44-hour workweek, which were rarities in the notoriously employee-unfriendly garment industry. And GWG was able to market its clothing as union-made, which likely helped with its working-class customer base.

The company grew quickly. Within a year, it had more than 100 employees, most of whom were women, as clothing was one of the few industries that would employ them at the time. In 1917, the company moved to a new factory in a former department store on 97 Street and 103 Avenue. GWG continued to grow throughout the 1920s, expanding both its workforce and its factory. During the 1930s, the company weathered the Great Depression by adding lines for women's wear and children's clothing, as well as making uniforms for city workers.

By the time the Second World War broke out, GWG was reputed to be the largest garment manufacturer in the British Empire. During the war, the company's workforce swelled to 500, and it was producing up to 12,500 uniforms a week. Most of them were destined for the Canadian military, but GWG also sent tens of thousands of garments across the Atlantic to outfit the Netherlands' armed forces in 1946. The emphasis on military uniforms and cotton rationing caused a shortage of GWG clothing in retail stores. The company still advertised heavily, telling customers that their garments were durable enough to last them through until peacetime.

During the war years, the company also put a great emphasis on efficiency and speeding up the manufacturing process. This philosophy continued into the post-war years, with GWG quick to adopt new technologies and seek automation whenever possible. It also saw the company open a 100,000-sq.-ft. factory on 85 Street in 1953.

GWG is also credited with several firsts in the history of blue jeans. It was the first in Canada to sell pre-shrunk jeans in the 1920s, and the first to sell pre-washed jeans, called Scrubbies, in 1972. They became one of the company's most popular products.

Jeans giant Levi Strauss bought a large portion of GWG in 1961, and then gained full ownership in 1972. The '80s and '90s saw the company lose much of its share in the Canadian jeans market, as competition rose. Rounds of layoffs marked those decades, and the new owners shifted some parts of production to factories in Ontario and Mexico.

Finally, in 2004, Levi Strauss shut down all of its North American factories. Four hundred and eighty-eight Edmonton workers were laid off, down from GWG's peak workforce of 1,600. During its nine-decade history, Great Western Garment Company became one of Alberta's largest industrial employers and introduced many innovations — both technical and related to labour conditions — into the garment industry.

The former GWG factory building on 97 Street is listed for lease after a number of attempted reuses, including as the site of the Downtown Farmers' Market from 2019 to early 2024. While Edmonton is no longer the hub of garment manufacturing it used to be, it is still home to various independent designers and manufacturers, many of whom are advocating for a more sustainable and local clothing industry.

This clipping was found on Vintage Edmonton, a daily look at Edmonton's history from armchair archivist Rev Recluse of Vintage Edmonton.

Gen Zers learn how to make a difference 'in a very intense time'

Sept. 3, 2026
By Stephanie Swensrude

A group of young activists spent a weekend networking and learning advocacy skills that organizers say will help ensure that youth perspectives are considered in decision-making.

"We are in these systems right now. Sure, in 30 years, we'll be where they are, but we're also here, and we deserve to have our asks and our rights protected and uplifted, just like anyone else," said Marilynn Burch-Harvey, co-founder of Dear Future YEG, the group that organized Youth ACCCTIVATOR on Aug. 15 and 16. "It's … empowering young people and just giving them that validation — 'You're angry, I'm angry too, you feel this way, we do too. What can we do about it?'"

Dear Future YEG was born out of Apathy is Boring's RISE program, which brings together youth looking to make a difference in their communities. "Originally, part of that was looking to connect youth with resources through a database," Burch-Harvey said. "We've kind of strayed away from that, and we've stuck more to doing events and bringing together community."

Many Gen Z youth are motivated to engage in politics and civic life, but they haven't learned the skills necessary to do so, Burch-Harvey said.

"We live in a very wild time — we live in a very intense time politically, socially, emotionally," Burch-Harvey said. "We're kind of all standing here, and there are so many things that people want to do, and there are so many communities that we want to advocate for and protect and uplift."

Attendees heard from a panel featuring Basel Abou Hamrah from the Newcomer Centre's Rainbow Refuge program, Saniya Ghalehdar of 1800SheSaid, Jannie Edwards of Amnesty International Edmonton, and NDP MLA Sharif Haji. They also participated in workshops led by Mariam Karmazanashvili of the United Nations Association in Canada, Yaw Baayim of the John Humphrey Centre for Peace and Human Rights, and Teagan Melnyk, an artist and advocate.

Sept. 3, 2026
By Mariam Ibrahim
  • Edmonton city council is considering additional funding for volunteer groups helping clean up Chinatown. Members of council's executive committee voted unanimously on Sept. 2 to develop a pilot program, which will be considered during upcoming four-year budget deliberations. A survey identified concerns including inconsistent cleanups, overflowing bins, illegal dumping and hazardous waste. The City currently has three cleanup teams serving Chinatown through its Centre City Optimization Program, with a combined budget of just over $1 million.
  • The City of Edmonton launched its Shop Local campaign amid rising prices and tensions over the Canada-U.S. trade war. The City said in a news release that residents can find promotions through the Shop Local Deals Directory. The City said 97% of nearly 30,000 businesses in Edmonton are small businesses and that $66 of every $100 spent at a small business stays in Edmonton's economy.
  • University of Alberta Hospital installed a weapons detection system at its emergency department entrance, becoming Edmonton's second ER with this screening after Royal Alexandra Hospital installed one earlier this year. Patients and visitors now have to pass through screening, with secondary checks when the system flags possible prohibited items.
  • The historic former Downtown YMCA is nearing the end of a $35-million redevelopment after almost nine years of work. Renamed Williams Hall, the building will open 90 affordable one-bedroom units in late fall, along with commercial and office space. Beljan Development acquired the property around 2018, but construction was delayed by the pandemic before resuming in 2023 with $15.05 million in government funding. The project preserves elements of the decades-old building, including remnants of its former swimming pool.
  • The Edmonton Police Commission moved its remaining 2026 public meetings online and paused in-person public speakers, citing safety concerns after disruptions at a July meeting, when public speakers criticized Edmonton Police Service Chief Warren Driechel's trip to Israel. Written submissions will continue to be accepted, and the commission will revisit the policy change in 2027.

Police said the allegations also involved damage at two LRT stations and ATB Place.

Art collective opens at Kingsway Mall in response to ADAP

Sept. 2, 2026
By Darcy Hoogers

A new art store at Kingsway Mall aims to make it easier for former AISH recipients to transition into employment under the new Alberta Disability Assistance Program.

Set to officially open on Sept. 8, the Prospect Art Collective store will help adults with mental health challenges acquire employment experience in a supportive and flexible environment. The social enterprise is part of the Retail Mental Health Program from Prospect, a 30-year-old non-profit dedicated to overcoming barriers to employment.

"We recognized that there was going to be an awful lot of people going into an employment situation that they weren't necessarily prepared for," program manager Lorraine Henderson told Taproot. "(ADAP) was one of the reasons why we came up with this program … (as) a lot of people with disabilities of any sort were going to be told that they were expected to be looking for employment."

Over the summer months, Henderson's team has been preparing the art store to be a space where participants can develop skills and confidence. Participants will be able to practice customer service, organizing merchandise and inventory, and supporting various tasks on the floor or behind the scenes. They'll also work on skills such as writing résumés and cover letters.

Henderson believes those who have been outside the workforce for extended periods of time have valuable skills that employers look for. But extra support may be needed to make it possible to get and keep a job. That's where Prospect comes in.

"We don't just send them out with a kick in the pants and say 'Here's your job, get to it,'" Henderson said.

As of July 1, nearly 80,000 Albertans who previously qualified for Assured Income for the Severely Handicapped were shifted to the Alberta Disability Assistance Program. ADAP recipients will receive less than they did on AISH but are allowed to earn more before their benefits are affected. The change has been heavily criticized by disabled Albertans and advocates, and its implementation has been rocky.

As advocate Zachary Weeks put it, AISH is for those whose disabilities permanently prevent employment, while ADAP is for those whose disabilities "substantially impede employment," and the latter will be expected to seek work.

"Many disabled Albertans want to work," Weeks wrote. "The concern is what happens when government adjudicators or contracted employment providers misunderstand someone's disability, overestimate their ability to work or fail to provide the accommodations and supports they need."

Sept. 2, 2026
By Mariam Ibrahim
  • The former Edmonton Journal building at 10006 101 Street NW is up for sale as an investment or owner-user property, with the listing describing it as suitable for adaptive reuse or redevelopment. The five-storey, 148,640-square-foot building, constructed in 1990, sits on a 0.86-acre site at 101 Street and MacDonald Drive and is currently vacant. The building, listed $3.26 million USD by CBRE, went on the market on Aug. 6.
  • Edmonton city council's urban planning committee approved higher road-closure fees during a meeting on Sept. 1, with the changes taking effect Jan. 1, 2027. The daily permit fee will rise to $32 from $25, while residential builders will pay a standard $185 fee. The changes aim to shorten construction-related disruptions, and BILD Edmonton Metro supported the revised system, saying daily fees should encourage builders to stay on schedule.
  • The City of Edmonton is renewing its heritage plan for the first time in 17 years, expanding it to include natural, Indigenous and community heritage alongside existing building heritage. The Edmonton Heritage Council said the update will create new ways for African, Caribbean and South American communities to participate in Edmonton's history.
  • The Connaught Armoury in Old Strathcona — a century-old building that once housed a military regiment, then a nightclub, and most recently a Youth Empowerment and Support Services drop-in centre — is listed for sale at $2.47 million. Provincial and municipal historic designations protect it from demolition.
  • About 124,000 Edmonton Public Schools students returned to classes on Sept. 1, with Edmonton Police Service and school staff on site to remind drivers to slow down in school zones. Staff and students expressed excitement for a "normal" school year after last year's began with a strike.
  • Edmonton Public Schools has cancelled all international field trips for the school year, citing civil unrest, fuel shortages, public health concerns and ongoing military conflicts. The move is part of a broader trend, with multiple school boards across Canada restricting or banning international travel.
  • A new high school created by the Northern Alberta Mikisew Cree First Nation opened in Edmonton this fall in a temporary space, welcoming Grade 10 students and teaching the Cree language alongside the standard Alberta curriculum. The permanent Rita Marten Nihiyawiwin Kiskinwamatowin High School is under construction on Whyte Avenue and is expected to be complete by early next year.
  • A former Edmonton transit peace officer was sentenced to two years of house arrest after pleading guilty to impersonating an Edmonton Police Service officer and using that guise to obtain a key to a woman's home. He was originally charged with housebreaking and sexual assault, but the sexual assault charge was dropped before sentencing.
  • Elections Alberta has begun mailing out special ballots for the Oct. 19 provincial referendum after receiving 225,000 requests — nearly four times the number from the 2023 provincial election. The ballots cover 10 questions, including whether to hold a binding referendum on Alberta separation. Albertans can apply for special ballots online until Oct. 9.

Bike routes cancelled or put off despite council direction

Sept. 1, 2026
By Stephanie Swensrude

Even though a council committee has told administration to proceed as planned with Edmonton's active transportation network expansion, regardless of parking and traffic concerns, administration has cancelled or deferred bike infrastructure in Grovenor, Terrace Heights, and along 95 Avenue in the west end.

Such moves have prompted a city councillor to seek funding options to complete routes that were approved in the current budget cycle, including those three, as well as to continue expanding the network from 2027 to 2030. And the Edmonton Bike Coalition is encouraging cyclists to take the road this week to demonstrate what the city would look like without bike lanes.

Ward Métis Coun. Ashley Salvador is set to introduce a motion at the Sept. 2 executive committee meeting to direct administration to bring forward two funding profiles during the 2027-2030 budget deliberations. The first would increase funding to finish off the routes planned in the 2023-2026 budget cycle. The second would allow the city to introduce another new round of active transportation infrastructure as informed by an update to the current implementation guide, to be presented to council ahead of budget deliberations.

At its Aug. 26 meeting, infrastructure committee heard an update on the routes planned in the 2023-2026 budget cycle. Administration had recommended that council proceed with only 13 remaining routes and reevaluate 14 others that would affect parking or vehicle lanes, to respond to community pushback and expected provincial legislation. Instead, councillors simply received the report for information, leaving the previously approved active transportation network expansion program in place.

However, the city's active transportation network expansion webpage indicates that infrastructure in Terrace Heights along 101 Avenue that was originally planned for 2026 is now under review until next year as administration analyzes how it will impact vehicle traffic. Infrastructure along 95 Avenue has been deferred as administration reviews impacts on parking and vehicle traffic, with no posted timeline for completion. Planned work in Grovenor has been outright cancelled after some residents raised concerns. The webpage said this is "due to community and council feedback about the loss of parking and changes to travel patterns" required for the unprotected bike pathways planned for the neighbourhood, adding that active transportation connections may be considered in future renewal opportunities.

Administration says it has delegated authority to make some design and routing changes in response to technical considerations and public feedback. To Salvador, that authority should not be used to prioritize parking and vehicle movement over active transportation goals.

"That's why this was an important conversation, to be very clear around what the expectations are from council around the criteria that we're using when we are continuing to build out bike infrastructure, and that heavily weighting parking and travel lanes at the expense of active transportation is not the intention," Salvador told Taproot.

Transportation minister Devin Dreeshen has signalled that he will introduce legislation that limits a municipality's ability to install bike lanes, especially if they take away vehicle parking or travel lanes. Given that context, deferred routes might never be built if the city doesn't act quickly, said Aaron Budnick, a volunteer with the Edmonton Bike Coalition. "With the legislation that's potentially coming up from the UCP, any delay on a project could mean that it's cancelled, effectively."

Headlines: Sept. 1, 2026

Sept. 1, 2026
By Mariam Ibrahim
  • The City of Edmonton is temporarily closing 121 Street at Yellowhead Trail from Sept. 1 to the end of November as part of the Yellowhead Trail Freeway Conversion program, as crews work to keep the project on schedule following heavy summer rain delays. Drivers should expect increased traffic on nearby routes, including 97 Street, 107 Street, 127 Street, St. Albert Trail and 118 Avenue.
  • The City of Edmonton confirmed 17 cases of Dutch elm disease this year, with a newly established banded elm bark beetle playing a significant role in spreading the tree-killing fungus. Edmonton has about 90,000 elm trees making up 22% of its urban forest, and the disease can destroy a community's entire elm population within a decade.
  • Edmonton city councillors said they have no intention to reintroduce calcium chloride as a road de-icer after a committee heard the chemical's long-term costs — including vehicle and infrastructure corrosion — outweigh its short-term benefits. Mayor Andrew Knack acknowledged it had made streets safer in testing but said Edmontonians have consistently opposed its expanded use.

On the agenda: Snow, climate, heritage

Aug. 31, 2026
By Stephanie Swensrude

This week, councillors will review new climate action priorities, a proposed update to the snow-and-ice-control policy, and a new heritage places strategy.

There is a community and public services committee meeting on Aug. 31, an urban planning committee meeting on Sept. 1, and an executive committee meeting on Sept. 2.

Here are some key items on the agenda this week:

  • Administration will present an updated policy and program for snow and ice control after a scheduled review. Resources and service levels this winter are expected to remain consistent with previous years; however, council can choose to fund an enhanced service level starting in winter 2027-2028. Administration said the "well maintained city" service package would stabilize operations and create year-round positions to provide festival and event support, "ensuring consistent, high-quality services that keep Edmonton's economy moving throughout the year." Council will vote on the policy at a future meeting. During record snowfall in the winter of 2025-2026, Mayor Andrew Knack said he wanted to significantly increase funding for snow clearing.
  • A third-party review of the city's climate strategies and action plans highlighted the need for more focused actions, closer alignment with the municipal budget cycle, and better monitoring and evaluation, says a report set to be presented to executive committee. Administration has identified 27 action items in its update to the climate implementation priorities. The report says the first priority is to establish an ongoing and accountable relationship with Indigenous peoples regarding climate. The remaining priorities are divided into the following categories: buildings and land use, transportation, infrastructure, nature and water, and low-carbon energy and waste. About $257 million would be required to meet all 27 priorities, about half of which is planned to be presented for consideration in the 2027-2030 budget process. About $5 million can be met with existing budget, and the remaining $129 million has no planned or existing funding source. Administration said it will also transition the carbon budget to a more comprehensive climate budget, which will use the priorities as its basis and also evaluate all other city projects in the 2027-2030 budget for their contribution to both climate risk and emissions.
  • Urban planning committee will review the updated heritage places strategy following nearly two years of work. The proposed new heritage places strategy includes four pillars: natural heritage, Indigenous heritage, community and cultural heritage, and built heritage. Its guiding principles are to be inclusive, integrated, community-led, living and evolving, visible and accessible, and collaborative. The strategy is presented alongside a new council policy that outlines how the strategy will be implemented. A main goal of updating the strategy is to widen the definition of "heritage places" to include not just historic buildings, but also natural spaces, cultural landscapes, and community landmarks.

A moment in history: Aug. 28, 1957

Aug. 28, 2026
By Scott Lilwall

On this day in 1957, the Roxy Theatre was advertising its plan to play first-run films.

Edmonton has a long history of beloved theatres, both of the cinema and playhouse variety. But the Roxy is one landmark that belongs to both camps. When it opened its doors in 1938, it was a movie theatre.

The Roxy was the creation of Bill Wilson. His father had been the manager of the Capitol, Edmonton's first dedicated cinema. Wilson had spent some time working for the government, but lost his job during the Great Depression. So, he returned to the family business and commissioned well-known architect William G. Blakey to design the building — the city's only theatre west of 104 Street.

The Roxy's opening gathered a lot of attention. Despite the dismal economic times, Wilson wanted to offer a luxurious theatre experience. The Roxy boasted air conditioning, comfortable seating, and an eye-catching Moderne style. Opening night attracted a lot of attention, with glowing newspaper articles and prominent Edmontonians in attendance.

Wilson would manage the Roxy until 1941, before moving south of the river to oversee the Garneau Theatre. That same year, the theatre was leased to the Odeon chain. It was the first of several operator changes that would eventually turn the Roxy into a $2 theatre. In the 1970s, the building underwent extensive renovations.

In 1989, the Roxy switched to a different kind of show when it was acquired by Theatre Network and turned into a home for live theatre. (The boxy cinema design apparently made it very well suited to puppetry.) Another round of renovations in the early 1990s upgraded the stage, seating, and lighting. The theatre also became the home of NextFest, Edmonton's long-running multi-disciplinary arts festival.

In January 2015, a fire gutted the Roxy, devastating Edmonton's theatre community. Without its home venue, Theatre Network was forced to move to a temporary venue on Gateway Boulevard. But the Roxy was not gone forever. In 2018, the theatre company announced plans to rebuild the venerable venue. In 2022, the curtains opened on the new, resurrected Roxy Theatre, complete with a rehearsal space and a gallery for visual art.

The Roxy's return has been a welcome story in Edmonton's arts community, but it hasn't been without its issues. There is an ongoing dispute with the owners of an adjacent building, leaving the south wall unfinished and exposed to the elements.

After 27 years under the direction of Bradley Moss, Theatre Network's artistic direction is now in the hands of Jenna Rodgers, with David Cheoros as executive director. The mainstage season opens with Oh, Anne! in September.

Knack's faith in Edmonton Global remains, despite departures

Aug. 27, 2026
By Colin Gallant

Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack continues to believe in a regional approach to economic development, even though five municipalities have left Edmonton Global and three more are on their way.

"My view has always been we are stronger together … especially on the economic development side, and I think Edmonton Global is a great entity to deliver on that," Knack told Taproot. "But each municipality, they'll make their own choice on that."

Strathcona County, Fort Saskatchewan, Sturgeon County, Parkland County, and Devon all left in 2025. Leduc County voted to leave in December 2024; Gibbons did the same in November 2025, and Beaumont followed in December. A two-year notice period is required before they can formally exit. The other shareholders are Edmonton, the City of Leduc, Morinville, St. Albert, Spruce Grove, and Stony Plain.

The agency has now had Daryn Edgar at the helm as its second-ever CEO for close to a year, and it has unveiled new strategic and business plans that emphasize accountability and return on investment.

Shareholders in Edmonton Global pay fees based on their population and tax base. In 2024, the total amount was $5 million annually; Edgar told Taproot that each municipality's contributions have "stayed pretty steady" despite the departures, though adjustments may be coming.

Knack, who was appointed vice-chair of the shareholders group in May, said he understands that different municipalities have different priorities, and that may be a factor in decisions to exit, though Edmonton Global has worked to engage with them as individuals with specific assets. But you can't please everyone all the time.

"Unless you're going to put out almost unlimited money, you do have to prioritize," he said. "You do have to focus your resources on the areas that have the greatest opportunity for return on investment, and so I think that's the whole body of work that Edmonton Global is doing — recognizing that as much as it would be wonderful to try to be everywhere and do everything, that's not really practical."

Neither Beaumont nor Leduc County would comment on Edmonton Global's refresh, as Edgar has described it. As for Gibbons, Mayor Rick Henderson told Taproot his council has not been swayed. Edmonton Global's scope doesn't address the town's key hurdle for economic development: land suitable for major development. Annexation is what it would take to lure Gibbons back to Edmonton Global, Henderson said.

"For us to hit that global market and say, 'Hey, we have a perfect place, we're in close proximity to shipping, there's a great highway to get in and out of town, there's a great workforce around us,' and all that kind of stuff, definitely, we need some more land to attract that kind of industry."

Artist questions CKUA's stance on AI and music

Aug. 26, 2026
By Darcy Hoogers

An Edmonton-based experimental artist who uses AI in his creative process is disappointed that his music is no longer welcome on CKUA's airwaves. And Canada's first public radio station finds itself trying to walk a fine line as it develops a formal AI policy.

The story of Ryan McCourt, a sculptor who also creates music under the name The Synthesist, raises a very modern question: In an age when studio-grade music can be produced through the click of a few buttons, what should be played on the radio?

In January, McCourt was overjoyed to hear his music played on Discoveries, an eclectic show hosted by Leo Cripps. "My music was the first thing played, and … I'm over the moon about that," McCourt recalled to Taproot.

In late May, McCourt made a donation to CKUA to directly support an hour of programming for Cripps's show. He provided a list of suggested songs, including two tracks from The Synthesist, created with the help of generative AI. (After this story was published, CKUA clarified that donors may not request a song that benefits themselves or a family member, due to charitable donation rules set by the Canada Revenue Agency.)

On June 2, Cripps wrote to McCourt to say CKUA's policy was to refrain from airing AI-assisted music, conceding that the station was still discussing AI's place in the world of art and music. This surprised McCourt, noting that such a policy did not appear to be publicly available, nor was there a definition of what constitutes AI-generated music. He also felt a blanket ban on music interfered with hosts' autonomy to select music for their programs.

"I have no argument with Leo because he's … got a job to keep, so he's doing what's required of him by his employers," he said. But he disagrees with CKUA's direction. "It's just giving incentive to people to not disclose that sort of thing, to not be honest about it."

On June 11, CKUA published a statement about AI-generated music. Following "conversations internally and with our community, we have made the decision to not knowingly play AI-generated music on CKUA," the statement says, noting CKUA's commitment to supporting artists and art workers. "Playing AI-generated music raises broader questions around authenticity, attribution, copyright, and the value we place on human creative expression." The statement goes on to say that CKUA is developing a formal policy that will be shared "when it is ready."

Listeners on "both fronts" of the AI debate are seeking clarity about CKUA's stance, content director Arianne Smith-Piquette told Taproot. The line between AI as a tool and AI as a replacement for the artist is one of the nuances that CKUA aims to make clear in its policy. And since the policy would affect CKUA's entire organization, including departments that use AI tools to maximize efficiency, CKUA is taking its time to get it right, she added. "I don't have an (estimated time of arrival) on it right now."

Smith-Piquette maintains that human creation must remain at the core of music at CKUA. However, defining what "human creation" means can be elusive. McCourt said he used Suno, a system that generates music from human prompts. Suno has landed Anthropic in legal trouble over the materials it was trained on and has resulted in a flood of AI-generated music on streaming services. McCourt said he also took time and care to edit and splice tunes together, using less controversial tools such as GarageBand.

"There's tons in the whole production experience that I went through that is on the cutting room floor," McCourt said. "It's not just like, 'Please make me a song,' (and) boop, a song comes out."

On the agenda: Bike lanes, climate resilience, Low Level Bridge

Aug. 24, 2026
By Stephanie Swensrude

This week, councillors are set to discuss a pause on future bike lanes that take away parking or travel lanes, amendments to the city's climate resilience policy, and early designs for the Low Level Bridge replacement.

There is a utility committee meeting on Aug. 24, a public hearing on Aug. 25, and an infrastructure committee meeting on Aug. 26.

Here are some key items on the agenda this week:

  • Administration has proposed pausing planned active transportation infrastructure that takes away parking spaces or vehicle travel lanes because of expected provincial legislation, as well as community pushback. A report due at infrastructure committee said that because the previous council chose the "rapid" approach to building bike lanes and other active transportation infrastructure, public engagement was limited and adaptable infrastructure was often used. The report said this has garnered significant negative feedback and pointed specifically to the recent decision to redesign infrastructure on 50 Street. The new design — retaining parking and vehicle travel lanes — costs about double the initial construction costs. Alberta Transportation Minister Devin Dreeshen spoke to residents in Capilano about that project in July. Dreeshen applauded a recent Ontario court decision that overturned an earlier ruling that stopped the provincial government from replacing protected bike lanes with car lanes in Toronto. "The appeal court made clear that governments have the authority to make and change transportation policy and that there is no constitutional right to a bike lane," Dreeshen wrote. Though the provincial legislation limiting active transportation infrastructure doesn't yet exist, the city report said making a proactive decision could help mitigate legal implications, which will be discussed in camera. The change in direction requires council approval; infrastructure committee is expected to give a recommendation to council, which will make the final decision at a future meeting. Additionally, administration is in the process of updating the Active Transportation Implementation Guide, which will be presented to council before the four-year budget deliberations. Administration has already cancelled planned infrastructure in Grovenor. That project didn't involve separated bike lanes, but rather traffic calming features and reduced parking.
  • Administration has prepared amendments to the climate resilience policy that incorporate the optimal point for capital investment that yields the best return for taxpayers when considering economic, environmental, and social benefits. The proposed change introduces a sustainable return on investment (S-ROI) analysis, meaning that projects would incorporate climate-resilient requirements to a point where a positive S-ROI is demonstrated, the report said. While this responds to financial constraints, it could also result in reduced environmental outcomes, meaning alternative solutions may be required to meet the city's emissions targets, administration said. The policy update also includes a new community adaptation target, which would combine data across multiple climate hazards to provide a measurable, citywide view of risk related to climate change. This work involves tracking the climate risk and adaptation of individual neighbourhoods. Fifty-seven neighbourhoods have a high or very high climate risk, and administration aims to reduce that number to zero by 2050. Infrastructure committee will review the changes before council makes the final decision at a future meeting.
  • Administration has released its preliminary plans for replacing the Low Level Bridge. A report set to be presented at infrastructure committee said that the city will likely build a functional roadway bridge rather than a "signature" structure. The report added that the initial traffic analysis suggested the replacement may need more than four lanes, but to align with city goals of reducing the number of people who use cars to meet their daily needs, a four-lane bridge will be considered. The alignment is expected to be to the west of the existing bridge. Administration had initially said the Low Level Bridge replacement project could involve simplifying the road network surrounding the bridge, as well as daylighting Mill Creek. However, this report says the replacement can be done without reconfiguring the road system. Public engagement will begin in the fall; the report notes that there are "no immediate risks when moving forward with only the Low Level Bridge replacement work at this time." Starting in 2027, the northbound bridge is expected to close for a construction season for repairs, and administration will create the preliminary design for the replacement bridge. Construction is expected to take place from 2029 to 2031. The following year, the southbound bridge is expected to be decommissioned and the northbound one converted to active transportation.

This week's batch of calls for public engagement includes a paid research project about multi-modal transportation, an open house about a new neighbourhood in Fort Saskatchewan, and an invitation to join advisory boards in Beaumont.

The City of Edmonton is recruiting residents to understand how people combine different modes of transportation, such as bicycles and e-scooters, with rides on the Edmonton Transit Service. A recruitment survey is open until Aug. 28.

Selected participants will be asked to complete a one-on-one virtual interview. Depending on their travel habits, they may be asked to document a full multi-modal trip. The city says combining different modes of active transportation is "a great way and green way to get around the city."

Edmonton's LRT design policies require multi-modal connections. The city's urban LRT approach calls for stronger links to walking, cycling, and the broader transit network, while its sustainable urban integration principles include shared-use pathways, sidewalks, trails, bike lanes connected to the existing bike network, and pedestrian-friendly zones around stops and stations.

There is bike parking at many transit centres around the city. There is also a secure storage facility at Century Park Transit Centre that is only accessible with a scan card, along with storage lockers at the South Campus/Fort Edmonton Park and Leger transit centres.

It's also possible to take bikes with you on your journey. Every bus in the city — except for Route 560, Route 747, and On Demand Transit buses — has a bike rack on the front. Riders can also bring bikes and shared e-scooters and e-bikes on the LRT at any time.

A moment in history: Aug. 21, 1926

Aug. 21, 2026
By Scott Lilwall

On this day in 1926, one of Edmonton's newest funeral homes was advertising its services.

Funeral services are now a big business. But in the early days of Edmonton, death was a smaller, more private affair. Before the 20th century, the deceased's body would be prepared at home, where the visitation and funeral would be held. A coffin would be purchased from a cabinetmaker or carpenter, and the body would be taken to the cemetery by wagon.

In 1908, Connelly-McKinley Funeral Home became the first such establishment in the city — and the province. The Andrews Brothers opened their own funeral business in the same year. These early funeral companies were run out of commercial storefronts downtown, mixed in with general stores and other retail shops. In addition to providing embalming services, these businesses would also handle transporting the body to the burial site using dedicated horse-drawn hearse wagons (or, during the winter months, hearse sleighs).

As the city's population grew, more funeral homes opened to address the demand. And that demand was higher in some years than others. Funeral services and cemeteries were overwhelmed in 1918, when a flu epidemic led to many deaths, leading to accusations of price gouging among some Alberta coffin builders.

The 1920s and '30s saw some big shifts in Edmonton's death industry. More funeral homes opened, including Howard and McBride in 1921. The industry was moving away from horse-powered hearses and into automobiles. (Many of which were also used as ambulances, meaning some people would get two rides in short order.)

Edmonton's funeral homes also began moving away from their storefronts on Jasper Avenue, creating stand-alone chapels and parlours meant to provide a quiet, more sombre atmosphere for viewings. Connelly-McKinley and Howard and McBride both moved to new buildings on 109 Street just south of Jasper, with the latter building a 135-seat, air-conditioned chapel.

Some of the city's original funeral homes are still operating, while others have closed or been bought up. The Howard and McBride chapel at 10045 109 Street NW closed down in 1988; the building housed several restaurants and bars until it was torn down in 2009.

The way Edmontonians choose to be remembered has changed. Cremations have become much more popular, with the vast majority of people in the city choosing that option instead of a casket burial in 2025. Interest in green burials has also risen, which allows bodies to decompose without embalming or grave liners. The city currently offers green burials at the Northern Lights Cemetery. The Royal Alberta Museum has much more to say about funeral practices in its Death: Life's Greatest Mystery exhibit, which runs until Sept. 7.

'Beyond Barriers' report explores challenges of 2SLGBTQ+ founders

Aug. 20, 2026
By Stephanie Swensrude

Queer and trans people in Edmonton often choose entrepreneurship out of necessity, and support that takes their identities into account is needed, says a new report from the Alberta 2SLGBTQI+ Chamber of Commerce.

"Queer folks and trans folks are more likely to hit barriers within established organizations, what we call a 'lavender ceiling,'" said Elli McDine, the chamber's executive director. "They may not be able to move forward, and so they may become frustrated within larger organizations and decide that they want to become their own boss."

While trans and queer people can be pushed to leave traditional careers because of ceilings or discrimination, the pull towards entrepreneurship can often be because they are their own first customer, McDine told Taproot. For example, a transmasculine person might start a business after designing a better binder to flatten the chest. Or a family might create an event space that not only tolerates queer and trans people, but celebrates them.

But navigating the business world, whether it's to obtain a business licence or access grant funding, can be challenging for someone who might not have institutional knowledge or a support system around them, says the report, which McDine's organization produced with Action Lab

To help close that gap, the chamber will be launching an interactive resource guide in September, and McDine said she will meet with policy-makers over the coming months to contextualize the report's findings within government systems. There will also be a networking and social event at Frank's Community Pub on Aug. 22 after the Edmonton Pride parade, with an information session on how to join Rainbow Registered, an accreditation program for 2SLGBTQI+-friendly spaces.

When entrepreneurs seek funding, some might have to decide between coming out yet again or refraining from centring that part of their identity. "Sometimes you're leaning in and saying, 'I'm a queer trans woman, and I live in Edmonton, and this is the kind of thing I'm trying to build,'" McDine said. "But if I'm going into a different grant or a different funding body, I might leave that element off because I'm worried that it may count against me."

Research from the Women's Enterprise Organizations of Canada found that a third of queer and trans entrepreneurs hide their identities professionally, and a quarter face discrimination or lose opportunities due to being out. None of the small business founders in Edmonton that the chamber spoke to had ever accessed a conventional small-business loan.

Edmonton Global's refresh aims to lift 'veil of unhappiness'

Aug. 19, 2026
By Colin Gallant

Armed with a new strategic plan and knowledge gleaned from many conversations, the head of the agency responsible for attracting foreign investment to the Edmonton metro region says she is focused on the individual needs of member municipalities.

"I kind of began from the (idea that) people are just people; I'm going to go talk to people," Edmonton Global CEO Daryn Edgar told Speaking Municipally. "Every person was constructive. They were forthcoming about the details and the attributes for their specific region and what ROI meant to them. It's not the same for every region; it's different because every region has different assets, they have different credentials, and they have different economic positions."

Edgar became CEO of the regional economic development agency in October 2025, replacing Malcolm Bruce, who had retired in March as five of 14 stakeholders were about to confirm their exit from the organization. Strathcona County, Fort Saskatchewan, Devon, Sturgeon County, and Parkland County all left in 2025. Leduc County voted to leave in December 2024; Gibbons did the same in November 2025, and Beaumont followed in December. A two-year notice period is required before they can formally exit. The other shareholders are the City of Leduc, Morinville, St. Albert, Spruce Grove, Stony Plain, and, of course, Edmonton.

One of Edgar's first duties was to meet with the mayors, chief administrative officers, and other key municipal staff from each shareholder, regardless of whether they were departing. She learned that dissatisfaction is not uniform.

"There are lots of different kinds of happy, and there are lots of different kinds of unhappy, specifically, for each specific shareholder — what is the happy and the unhappy?" Edgar pondered as she met with them. "I've got to say, I did come into a situation where there was this veil of unhappiness, and it was really opaque."

Spruce Grove Mayor Jeff Acker is optimistic about Edmonton Global now that Edgar is at the helm and the agency has new strategic and business plans. Treating municipalities as individuals while developing a cohesive region is beginning to pay off, he told Taproot's civic affairs podcast.

"I think we're relieved," he said. "We have identified some huge opportunities. We've streamlined the organization. We have way better accountability in reporting. I think, as a shareholder, we have good information now to share with our councils and our communities that we have a plan for the future."

Acker and Edgar both said the remaining and former stakeholders in Edmonton Global believe in regionalism as a way to attract foreign direct investment, but it hasn't always been easy to justify agency dues and their implications on tax assessments for residents and businesses. That's partly why the new plans from Edmonton Global emphasize accountability and return on investment.

"We're going to take our efforts and apply them to places where tax-base jobs and capital expenditures can be generated in the short term," Edgar said. "By the short term, I mean under 60 months, because we do have these very long close cycles. Market-making projects tend to get measured in years, whereas our close cycles are measured in months."

The best hire you haven't made yet

A message from CAREERS: The Next Generation:

On Sept. 28, Alberta marks Apprenticeship Day, a provincial recognition of the skilled tradespeople and apprentices who keep the economy running. For employers facing persistent labour shortages, the day is also a reminder of one of the most effective, and most overlooked, workforce development strategies available: building a strong program to mentor and develop apprentices in-house.

According to Stefan Rutkowski, president & CEO of CAREERS: The Next Generation, employers who invest in developing apprentices early are solving tomorrow's staffing problems today.

"Apprenticeship Day is a great moment to recognize the tradespeople who built this province, but it's also a call to action," says Rutkowski. "If you're an employer struggling to find skilled workers, the answer isn't always out there in the labour market. Sometimes it's about growing your own talent from within."

That's the philosophy behind CAREERS, a non-profit that has spent nearly three decades connecting Alberta youth with employers for paid internships and apprenticeships. The organization works directly with schools across the province, giving students exposure and a head start in the trades and other high-demand industries before they graduate.

"Engaging with youth while they're still in high school, or right after they graduate, gives employers an edge," Rutkowski says. "You get to help shape someone's skills early, build loyalty, and create a pipeline instead of scrambling to fill a position every time someone retires."

That pipeline is already paying off in Camrose, where DeeJay Plumbing and Heating has hired students through the Registered Apprenticeship Program since 2007. "We're talking 20% to 30% of our staff," says Clayton Appleby, the company's preconstruction manager, "and a lot of our core staff has come out of the program."

Dee Jay's project manager/estimator, Stephanie Schielke, is one of them. "I started in the Registered Apprenticeship Program 18 years ago, and now I'm helping to train the next generation of skilled workers," she says. "It feels amazing."

Rutkowski sees that as proof no single group builds a workforce alone. "It takes schools, employers, and communities pulling in the same direction," he says, "and that's exactly what's happening in places like Camrose."

To make that easier, CAREERS offers qualified employers up to $7,500 in funding to hire youth through the Youth Internship Incentive Program. Spots are limited, and Rutkowski encourages interested businesses to apply soon.

"We want to help as many employers as possible bring on an apprentice this year," he says. "The funding takes some of the financial pressure off, but the real value is what that apprentice brings to your team long after the funding runs out."

In addition, CAREERS' services, from matching businesses with vetted, work-ready youth to supporting the paperwork behind funding applications, are entirely free.

"We get there are also challenges with mentoring youth, but the vast majority of our employer partners understand it's worth it. We exist to make it as easy as possible for employers to get started," Rutkowski says.

As Alberta celebrates the tradespeople shaping its future this Apprenticeship Day, CAREERS is encouraging employers across the province to think about the apprentice they could be training next. Find out more at www.careersnextgen.ca.

Carbon-capture project on hold at Edmonton cement plant

Aug. 18, 2026
By Darcy Hoogers

Diminished interest in incentivizing reductions in carbon dioxide emissions has delayed an Edmonton project once touted to be the world's first cement plant with full-scale carbon capture and storage.

In 2023, Heidelberg Materials signed a partnership with the federal government to support a $1.36-billion project to bring a full-scale carbon capture, utilization, and storage system to its cement plant in northwest Edmonton. The company said then that it would be capturing 1 million tonnes of C02 annually by the end of 2026.

But the project, which the federal government called "a major step forward in establishing Canada as a global leader in the production of low-carbon concrete," is not on track to be done this year, despite a successful pilot of the technology, and it's not clear when it will be.

The price of carbon emissions is "not an insignificant" element when determining the viability of a full-scale CCS project, said David Perkins, vice-president of sustainability and public affairs for Heidelberg Materials.

"Originally there was discussion around $170 a tonne by 2030," he told Taproot. "The (federal) government has backed off of that now. The province has backed off of that to a much lower level."

Coun. Keren Tang was surprised to hear that the carbon-capture project was delayed when she toured the plant during the Pacific Northwest Economic Region summit in July.

"(Heidelberg said) we're not quite there yet, and I think that's true for … a lot of other developments that had a lot of excitement, but were slowed down because of the market, because of global trends, because of policy," Tang said in an interview. "I was just a bit surprised because I haven't had that update, but it was good that (Heidelberg was) able to answer some of our questions."

In the meantime, Heidelberg's CCS project at a cement plant in Norway was completed last year, making it the world's first.

On the agenda: Gorman, Garneau, Girard

Aug. 17, 2026
By Stephanie Swensrude

This week, Edmonton city council will discuss rezoning applications in the new neighbourhood of Gorman and the old neighbourhood of Garneau, as well as in the Girard Industrial area for a wellness facility.

There is a public hearing on Aug. 17, a council meeting on Aug. 18 and 19, and a special city council meeting on Aug. 21.

Here are some key items on the agenda this week:

  • Council will review broad planning documents for the future Gorman neighbourhood in north Edmonton, which is envisioned as a transit-oriented community built around an LRT stop. The developer proposed amendments to the area structure plan and neighbourhood structure plan to re-designate some areas for higher density than what is currently allowed. Administration said the application is an improvement to the plan because it maintains the NSP's vision of a transit-oriented community while providing more opportunities for medium- and high-density uses in logical areas served by amenities.
  • The Hope Mission has submitted a rezoning application for a lot at 7011 Girard Road NW, to allow for an emergency shelter and wellness facility that would support up to 125 people experiencing homelessness. Some nearby residents said they oppose the facility because they think it would bring crime to the area; they also cited the site's proximity to Pure Casino Edmonton on Argyll Road as well as liquor and cannabis stores, which could conflict with the path to recovery for occupants.
  • Council will review a rezoning application for a property in Garneau that would allow for increased site coverage, an additional 2.5 metres in building height, and a reduced rear setback. Administration said it supports the application because the scale of development is appropriate within the University major node and provides additional housing units near local businesses, open space, school sites, and active transportation. Some Garneau residents said they oppose the rezoning because the proposed development would alter the historic character of the area and preempt the Garneau Community League's pending proposal to designate part of the neighbourhood as a special character heritage area.

Headlines: Aug. 17, 2026

Aug. 17, 2026
By Mariam Ibrahim
  • The Alberta Avenue Business Association is urging city council to find a way to charge vacant commercial properties the same BIA levy businesses pay, arguing empty buildings can attract disorder while owners get a tax break. Mayor Andrew Knack said administration is examining whether empty sites could be treated as pending businesses.
  • Downtown Edmonton businesses told a public safety forum they are paying for cameras, repairs, and extra security while asking governments for more help with vandalism, break-ins, and visible drug use. The Downtown Revitalization Coalition said increased police patrols helped but did not solve the broader problem.
  • Edmonton Public Library said in a release that Canada Place Child Care Society will move into the Stanley A. Milner Library this fall and rebrand as Early Chapters Child Care Society. The library said the third-floor space will include a kitchen, gym area, and secure outdoor play yard.
  • Edmonton Transit Service riders should expect Capital Line LRT disruptions from Aug. 22 to 24. Trains will not run between Churchill and Clareview stations on Aug. 22 and 23 or between Coliseum and Stadium stations on Aug. 24. Replacement buses will run every seven minutes until 7pm, then every 10 minutes.
  • Edmonton is seeing widespread erosion and slope failures after months of heavy rain, more than two decades after the 1999 Whitemud Road landslide, Postmedia reported. Saturated soil and July downpours have damaged roads, bridges, trails and riverbanks, while experts warn increasingly extreme weather could make erosion harder and more costly to manage.
  • The Edmonton Police Service is investigating the suspicious death of a 16-year-old girl in northeast Edmonton on Aug. 16. Officers responded to a shooting, where they found the girl seriously injured. She died at the scene. Police said the homicide section is investigating.
  • The Alberta Court of Justice will rename Gladue reports as Indigenous background reports starting Sept. 1 after consulting members of the Gladue family, Indigenous leaders, and court workers. The court said the change does not alter the reports' purpose of giving judges fuller context at sentencing.
  • The Alberta government has postponed new school flag rules, while draft regulations show schools would be allowed to fly Alberta and Canadian flags, sports flags, municipal flags, Vatican City, and some Treaty and foreign flags for limited periods, Postmedia reported. The draft does not mention Pride flags.
  • Support sessions for people seeking compensation under the federal Indian hospitals class-action settlement are coming to Edmonton this week, with free claims help plus wellness and cultural supports for survivors of abuse at segregated hospitals, including the Charles Camsell Indian Hospital. The settlement can pay eligible claimants between $10,000 and $200,000.
  • A Court of King's Bench judge has cleared the way for a Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation judicial review over a water licence tied to the proposed Wonder Valley AI data centre near Greenview. The First Nation argues Alberta had a duty to consult before approving annual diversion of six million cubic metres from the Smoky River.
